utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom, after having been absent for quite a while. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We are meeting today to have the pre-Defence conference. I have an agenda and I'd like to go through it, and at the very end you have an opportunity to add whatever is needed to be added. I'd like to start with the technical issues that were raised recently. And I would first like to invite the Defence to give the Chamber an update as to the progress that has been made with regard to the technical issues it has been experiencing up till the moment of this conference. Mr. Lukic, any problems remaining or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask Your Honours to ask Mr. Ivetic if -- since he's really more in charge of this aspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, any problems -- technical problems remaining and if so which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's a little hard to say which ones remain. I do know that the IT staff was -- five individuals were in the Defence rooms as of last Wednesday or Thursday continuing to address problems with individual computers on the various log ins. I don't know which problems exist on which computers since my log-in appears to be functioning. The -- I just spoke with some staff earlier this morning and I was -- I've been told that everything should be addressed this week and should be then functioning this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, there's no need for Mr. Mladic to stand unless there's any specific matter raised. Mr. Mladic, would you please sit down. You can sit down even if they are working on your computer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please sit down, Mr. Mladic, now, right away. And no loud speech either. Mr. Lukic, could you please remind Mr. Mladic if he wants to consult with you that he should do at an inaudible level, an inaudible volume of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. He just objected since nothing works on his desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you don't have to stand. There is no reason there. But, of course, it should be fixed and that's what the Chamber is always aiming at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The technician will arrive to assist, I do understand. Is Mr. Mladic able to follow the proceedings? Then I would suggest that we would continue. Mr. Ivetic? We'll wait for a second, although you can see the English text on the screen and a picture of the courtroom. There's no evidence on the screen at this moment. Is there any possibility to use another screen for Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were the problems fixed? They were. Then we'll continue. Mr. Ivetic, let's -- me resume where you said that ... Have the problems not been fixed? Then I'd like to be informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- could -- could someone inform the Chamber about what the problem still is, if there's any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told again the transcripts -- neither the transcript nor the monitor were working. I'm told now it is working again so we should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Do we have to understand the keen interest of Mr. Mladic that he is able to read English? Is that what we should understand from this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Lukic, or Mr. Ivetic, briefly report any problem remaining?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With the monitors here? No, I'm told it's working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Then let's proceed. And my question -- Mr. -- Mr. Mladic should not speak aloud. He should consult with counsel and then it should stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can report, Your Honours, that the monitor in front of the General is not functioning with the video. It only has the transcript. And therefore, he has to follow the video on one of the auxiliary monitors to the side of him. I don't know which one is turned towards him, but the monitor in front of him does not have anything but the transcript which he cannot follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever -- whatever is shown on the video of the courtroom, you can see with your own eyes if you are present in this courtroom. So, therefore, there seems really to be -- that seems to be a non-issue. Then we -- please proceed, Mr. Ivetic. You said that should then be functioning this week. The Chamber received reports saying that all the technical problems were fixed so that there was an ample opportunity to use whatever technical facilities that the Defence would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe most of the major issues have been fixed and we have been able to function in the manner in which we previously were not able to function. There are still, I believe, some issues with -- particular issues that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- that only arises when someone logs in on the computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have any details about that, the Chamber will hear about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll move on. At the 98 bis decision hearing, the Prosecution stated that many associated exhibits had not been uploaded into e-court and the Chamber wonders whether this has now been completed. Are there any other remaining e-court-related problems? Associated exhibits, all uploaded by now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: They were uploaded for the Defence at the time of the 98 bis. That was the batch that e-court -- the IT had a problem with. I'm told those are all uploaded and I presume that they're searchable to the Prosecution under 65 ter numbers. That would have been batch 108 that we dealt with at the 65 ter conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while it is true that we do have access to the associated exhibits for the initial witnesses, it seems that there are a large number of exhibits that still are not in e-court and there seems to be a large number of translations which are not in e-court. So as of yet, we're unable to -- to read them. So I think what Mr. Ivetic is saying is true for the first few witnesses but after that is untrue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we earlier discussed during the technical meeting that some 1700 - that was the number was mentioned - were uploaded but there might be a similar number which had not been uploaded yet and since the technical problems seem to have been resolved, the Chamber wonders what happened with the other exhibits still to be uploaded into e-court. What's their number and what's the reason if they're not uploaded that they are not uploaded? Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As Your Honour recalls from the 65 ter conference, we indicated that first the documents have to be collated from the various databases that we use and then needed to be checked against the system to see whether they are already in the system and then uploaded, assigned 65 ter numbers, and released. We are in the process of doing so and we hope by the end of this week to have a much better grasp of the number and to see if we are able to complete that task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this is then not caused any further by the technical problems, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is caused by the delay and the in-access that we had for two weeks to use the computers to perform these type of searches. We were unable to operate using e-court so as to check the documents to see if they're in the system, and that was the main problem that -- we therefore had a back-log of work that is in the process of still being dealt with by all members of the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter, but it is not clear yet whether the delay is exclusively caused by the technical problems we had at the time or whether there are other problems. The Chamber, of course, would like to be informed. If there are any organisational problems or -- then they might need a different response. Mr. Groome, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, closely related to this is the exhibit list itself. So the exhibit list that was received, the highest 65 ter number on it is 7024, but there are only 1.974 numbers enumerated in that. It also included the word "preliminary" in the exhibit list, so if we could have some clarification about the finality of the exhibit list and how many exhibits we can expect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is a preliminary exhibit list. We said it was going to be a preliminary exhibit list and that we are going to working on uploading the documents that -- once we get them processed. I again having not -- do not know the exact number of documents because there are documents that will be duplicates and there are documents that will be removed upon that review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the approximate number would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information, Your Honour. I'm not in a position to give an approximate number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many documents are there which you still have to check against duplicates.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thousands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thousands is anything between 1.000 and 100.000. Where do we stand approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told by my colleagues approximately 3 and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Total number or numbers still not being uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Still not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's approximately the double of what we heard during the technical meeting? I'm afraid that there's more than a technical problem. There seems to be a logistical and an organisational problem. Would the Defence agree with that? Because if so, we might have to not to call the technicians in but to further and more closely monitor what the real problem is. Is there an organisational problem apart from the small delays caused by a technical problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a large case with a large number of documents. We have a large number of tasks that members of the Defence team have been doing in the past several months including meeting with witnesses and trying to locate witnesses and trying to prepare statements for witnesses, Your Honours. It is, you know -- we have a limited number of persons and therefore the work that we do is limited by the number of persons that we have. We don't have a budget for more persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a long answer but the answer apparently is yes there's not just the technical problem but we are facing other problems, and apparently it's staffing rather than technicians to be blamed for what happens at this moment. The Chamber will further consider the matter. But, Mr. Groome, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is the Defence able to say when they think this process will be finished? We would like to have some idea about when we would expect some -- a more complete exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As I believe I indicated a few moments ago, we are in the process of doing that and we hope to have by the end of the week more documents uploaded and a new list prepared with those additional documents once they are released in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, do you really think that the information that by the end of the week you expect more documents to be uploaded to be of any use? I take it that it will not be less, it will not be the same, it will be more. But, of course, what we are trying to find out is where we stand in qualitative terms, and your answers are not of great assistance in getting a better picture of the problem and time needed to resolve it. Mr. Groome, apparently there's no answer yet. Mr. Ivetic, have you considered to upload documents taking the risk that there are duplicates and then strike the duplicates at a later stage? Which is better than to have no documents uploaded. And everyone could even help you in finding duplicates so that we could clean that list as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I could do that. The process then of uploading and of removing 65 ter numbers also takes time. I don't know -- that's not a task that I normally do so I don't know how long it takes to actually physically upload a batch of 5.000 pages or thereabouts and if that would assist in things moving faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I don't do things myself, I usually inquire with those who are doing it to find out the details which anyone else would need at this moment. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider during the first break whether a deadline should be set, and if any party would like to -- to say anything about those deadlines, they have an opportunity to do so now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I've been as precise as I'm able to. I don't want to mislead the Chamber or the Prosecution by stating something that I'm not 100 per cent factually accurate about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But you should have been prepared in such a way that you could give us the accurate factual information. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would the Prosecution's strong preference that an exhibit list, however imperfect, be filed as soon as possible, recognising that given these problems the Defence may seek to amend by removing duplicates at a later stage. But the Prosecution is in a very difficult position now not knowing what the exhibits are in proceeding, so I think the most fair resolution would be that the Defence file their list, recognising there may be some problems, may be some duplicates, and we'll work with that. At least we can begin our work having the benefit of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any response to this suggestion, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Only again to point out that if duplicates are input in the system, it means that someone will have to manually input the description of a document, the 65 ter number, the date, and the language multiple times which will take us longer to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just add if have a list, we do have some techniques where we could search that list and then perhaps even assist the Defence in finding duplicates. I can't make any guarantee of that. But having nothing, we don't know what the problem is and we don't if we can assist in any way and we're disadvantages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you mean if you have a list even if it's not yet fully uploaded into e-court that at least you'll have something in your hands could you start working with?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour, and we could try to run some of our procedures to look for duplicates and other problems with the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will check to see if we can accommodate that at least in part. I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you intend at this moment to upload documents, an exhibit list, in e-court, then, of course, you should have a list of the documents you intend - duplicates or not - to intend to be uploaded into e-court and to be part of the 65 ter exhibit list unless you have not made up your mind yet as to what documents you would like to select. And that's not a technical problem, that's an organisational problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: As I indicated in the Rule 65 ter conference, Your Honours, we have multiple lists. We have a list for every witness. And those individual lists are linked to documents and individual folders. Those documents then need to be digitally uploaded into e-court. The descriptions need to be input in e Scan-IT. And therein lies the problem: We don't have a single list until they are in included into e-court and get a 65 ter number. Before then we have a bulk of documents that are separated by witness that are identified according to the information that we have and that are -- that are digitally segregated or collated to be uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the preliminary list we see what appears to be some sequential number of the exhibits. We go up to 7024. If we can simply even have whatever that list is, that sequential list that has that information about the exhibits, at least we can make a start in our preparations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is not a sequential list going up to 7.000 exhibits. We had to skip ranges because of the problems we were having with batches. So we had to open new batches. When you open a new batch, we assigned numbers in a higher range so as not to run into them when the upload of the documents from the lists caught up to it; so, for instance, we had maps input into a particular batch and all given numbers in the, I think, 6.000 range, we had documents relating to experts into one range, we had documents relating to international witnesses in another range, and therefore those batches of exhibits -- of 65 ter documents were given 65 ter numbers in a different range of thousands of documents so as not to run over with the work of other people since we had multiple people work to go upload to try to accommodate the deadline given the -- given the delay that we encountered. And therefore, we have documents that are listed as 65 ter numbers 1D7000, I think even 1D8000, but that does not mean that we have -- that we have in between those 65 ter numbers assigned for other documents as of yet. We are in the process of collating and then putting those documents according to witnesses. We have multiple lists for those witnesses that we have already been able to organise those documents for. We do not have a central list until it is put into e-court and the 65 ter number is assigned at that point for a unique document and then that is generated and that is what we presented as the preliminary list which we filed the other week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider also whether it will instruct the Defence to just put together all the information, copy, paste send it to the Prosecution. I mean, this is not the way which allows for a useful continuation of the proceedings. Therefore measures will have to take. The Chamber will consider it. We'll move on. The Prosecution second response to the urgent Defence motion seeking to enlarge time contains some suggestions. I wonder whether we need to address them, but I'll just briefly go through them. If the Defence would need access to a non-network printer, this could be organised. Any need still for that, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, the printers were always -- are mainly functioning -- they're functioning as we speak, so I don't think that the stand-alone printer would at this stage add anything since we usually work with [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... The simple answer therefore is there is no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there was a suggestion by referencing Defence documents by both their Rule 65 ter number and their doc ID numbers during witness examination. That is a matter, I think, we should also deal with together with the Registry, so I leave it for the time as it is. Weekly technical reports were suggested by the Prosecution. The Chamber doesn't see the need for such a regular reporting schedule. At the same time, it may well be that whenever problems are there, it should be reported, irrespective of a weekly interval, and it now turns out that the Chamber is not updated in detail where it may have -- where there may have been some need to be informed about the problems. The Registrar informs me that although working with doc ID numbers is certainly not ideal, that it -- although imperfect, would still be workable. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the time the Prosecution made this recommendation it was our understanding that the -- the problems were limited to technical problems. It seems after this morning that there may be additional organisational and staffing problems. So I would amend our proposal to include a weekly report about those until such time as all of the disclosure and all of the obligations by the Defence have been met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood. I move away from these, I would say technical issues but they turned out to not be technical issues exclusively, and move on to the preliminary issues with regard to the Defence Rule 65 ter (G) witness list. The Chamber would have a few questions. One of the things that was noted by the Chamber is that Prosecution witnesses are included in the Defence witness list. I think we saw some eight Prosecution witnesses appearing on the Defence witness list, and the Chamber wonders what explains that. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: (redacted) and I believe RM255, were witnesses that Your Honours relied upon in the Rule 98 bis decision which, of course, indicates to the Defence that Your Honours are not apprising the testimony of these witnesses in the manner that we had expected from the cross-examination, so we then, as Your Honours will recall with RM255, we specifically did not go into one issue with the witness based upon the Prosecution stating that they were not going to be relying upon that evidence. And now we come to a situation where the witness is viewed as a credible witness despite that incredible aspect of his testimony that we did not address in cross-examination. With RM019, that is the situation that my colleague has just described and that is that witness. So in relation to the witnesses that we put on the list to call back, it was information that arose after they had testified here and after they had been cross-examined. I am aware of, I believe, four that fall into category, so I don't know the remaining four that Your Honours make reference to, whether those are indeed the document analyst that Mr. Lukic has mentioned and any one additional. I don't know the entirety of -- of witnesses on our list who would have been Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But wouldn't it be appropriate under those circumstances, Mr. Ivetic, to explain why the Defence wishes to call those witnesses against and seek permission to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe we did that in the summary on the 65 ter list, Your Honours. It lists for those witnesses precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But just putting reason on the list, is that asking for permission? There seems to be some --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand now. Yeah, no. I -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should have just filed --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- we should ask you to petition the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a request to be allowed to re-call witnesses that have been called again and giving the reasons for that so that you, depending on what the Chamber would decide, then can put those witnesses on your witness list. That's the appropriate procedure. And therefore either strike them or make such a request, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you want the numbers, we -- the -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is talking about the entries on your list, number 63, 68, 93, 127, 166, 229, 253, and 262, so I'm referring to the entries on the exhibit list. Mr. McCloskey, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President. Could we go into private session just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. A few more questions about the witness list. First, some witnesses are not named; I'm referring to entries 116, 313, and 314. Any explanation for that, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information we received about these three witnesses made us - in fact forced us - to ask for a postponement. It's characteristic for the Witness RM313 -- Could we please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Time estimates, Mr. Lukic, are missing for entries number 45, 62, 78, 104, 149, 171, 221, 260, 263, and 314. Any explanation for not having any allocated time estimates?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can answer for 314 easily; it's 92 bis, I think. And about the rest, I should -- I should check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me have a look. Yes, you're right, 314 is 92 bis, so that's mistake on our part. And the estimate is zero, therefore. And the others you said ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should check. Could you please do so as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are also a few witnesses where there are missing modes of testimony, and I'm referring to entries 127 and 263, I think, but let me just ... Any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Now we -- I would like to raise the following matter. We have received some Rule 92 ter motions and we have received these witness [indiscernible]. Now, the time allocation does not always correspond, which, of course, confuses us. If, for example, for witness entry number 5 the witness list says 45 minutes but the time in the 92 ter motion is 30 minutes, then we -- perhaps we could be happy that less sometime needed, but if we would then go to entry 42, it's just the opposite way around. There are at least a number -- of the only limited number of 92 ter motions we have received, I already have 12 or 13 not corresponding time estimates. Even going up three times ... three times the indication from the witness list in the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that everybody would be happier if we go with a shorter time. And if it's in the motion 30 minutes, it would be 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I mean to say, entry 150, the witness list gives 60 minutes and the time referred to in the motion is 180 minutes. That's two more hours. Three hours instead of one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, then, again, we'll go with the shorter time, 60 minutes, since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we can always take the shortest time. So instead of 92 ter 180 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we can take 60 minutes. Yes, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can explain if you need further explanation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- why that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I take it that's a matter of co-ordination and -- and that is especially what is of great concern to the Chamber. But if you wanted to say more about it, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were anticipating to have this witness viva voce instead of mixture of 92 ter and viva voce, and you are right there was lack of co-ordination between two branches of our team and that's why this confusion was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although we did it, the Chamber doesn't find it its duty to compare all the lists and to clarify what seems to be rather chaotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We accept that and we are grateful for your efforts, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly then that the 92 ter motion is being with withdrawn at this stage? I'm confused as to where we are at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, you do not have to understand it that way. He will testify as a mixed witness and we do not raise the time necessary for his direct. So 60 minutes with 92 ter motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That brings me to my next item on the list. I would like to recall that the Chamber gave guidance at the beginning of the Prosecution case that the examination-in-chief of Rule 92 ter witnesses should generally last 30 minutes, not more. The Chamber noticed that a number of witnesses on the Defence witness list have an estimated examination-in-chief time of one hour or more although being 92 ter witnesses. So apparently it seems that you have ignored, more or less, this limitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry if you understood it, Your Honours, that we ignored your guide-lines, but in the time-period we have -- we had, actually, in the field, we were able only to meet with the witness once. And we expect that it might occur that he will tell us during the proofing before the testimony something else or something more. So that's only the reserve those usually extra 15 minutes. Usually most of them, mixture witnesses, 92 ter and viva voce, and according to our list are scheduled for 45 minutes. If there is nothing new, and we hope there wouldn't be anything new, then we would, of course, stick with the guide-lines and lead our mixed witnesses only for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's of some concern to the Chamber that you qualify them already as mixed witnesses because the witness expects 92 bis witness, 92 ter witnesses, or viva voce witnesses where the Chamber accepts that there's always a possibility that something new comes up, but already to qualify them from the beginning as mixed witnesses saying that they may come up with something new confuses the system, and, therefore, the Chamber would like you to work on the basis of 92 ter or viva voce rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether we were confused by the -- our case where the Prosecution called them 92 ter viva voce or by Karadzic case, where -- and -- yeah, it's Milutinovic case also, both Mr. Ivetic and I were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This Chamber works along the lines set by this Chamber, and there are some slight -- there are some slight variation between the way in which chambers work. If you would compare some of the experience counsel may have had in cases I earlier presided over, especially in view of 92 ter, you'll see that this Chamber has taken an approach which is not exactly the same, and we work on the basis of our guidance. Okay. I leave it for the time. But 92 ter witnesses are still under the guidance of the 30-minutes' rule. Then -- but perhaps we would go into private session for the next two items, I would deal with, the last matters on the witness list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Groome you're on your feet, even before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to -- I rise. It seems that the Chamber is concluding its discussion of witness list. Could I ask over the break that the Defence consider whether GRM086 and GRM329 are in fact the same person. They appear to us to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For this reason alone, we'll take a break a little bit longer so as to afford such time. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will deal with a few matters we discussed before the break. As far as Prosecution witnesses appearing on the Defence witness list is concerned, I think I said strike them or make an application to re-call them. Now, that was not very accurate. My language was not accurate. Because they have to be stricken anyhow, because even if you would re-call them, they should not be on the Defence exhibit list. They are still Prosecution witnesses to be re-called for further examination. I clarify this so that the position of those witnesses is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then since the -- apparently the reasons why the Defence would wish to re-call them, if they do not -- after they've stricken them any of how, since these reasons are known already, the Chamber expects any application for re-call of those witnesses to be filed before the summer recess. Because you apparently have made up your mind as to why you would wish to re-call them, so, therefore, we are not going to wait until the end of the case. It would be -- it's appropriately done short-term; that is, before the summer recess. Then I think I earlier already withdrew the observation that for Witness 314 no time estimate was given. Rightly, the Defence brought to our attention that it was a 92 bis witness. The same is true for witnesses entry numbers 45, 104, and 149. So for four witnesses it's now perfectly clear why there is no time estimate because they're 92 bis witnesses. However, the remaining four are still not explained. And I would say that there even are a remaining five because it's all together not eight witnesses but nine witnesses for which no time was indicated. Number 64 is the one to be added to the remaining four. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope you'll give us a couple of days so we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- give it the time. But I -- probably those are 92 ter witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A couple of days is okay. But, of course, we need the witness list to be -- to become final. But I'll deal with that in a second. As far as the unnamed witnesses are concerned, the -- One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I made a mistake. When I referred to Witness 64 as the ninth, it was a witness actually which was not -- should not be added to the lists where there is no time estimate but it should be added to the list of Prosecution witnesses which still appear on the list and should be stricken from the list of the Defence witnesses and an application to re-call them to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mixed up a few things. First of all, I repeat that the ninth witness which appeared on the Defence witness list but was an OTP witness was number 64. Now, the witnesses for which still a estimate of time is missing, I just mention them now leaving out the 92 bis. The remaining witnesses are entry 62, 78, 171, 221, 260, and 263. That's now complete. I think I started talking about the anonymous witnesses. The Chamber will not accept any witness on the witness list which is without a known name. That means that if the names are not known that, that at this moment they should be removed from the witness list, and if there's any reason to add them later, the usual procedure applies; that is, the party should seek the approval of the Chamber to add them again to the list and give the reasons for the late addition. The Chamber sets a date for the witness list to be filed, and that is the 16th of May - that is, this Friday - close of business. The Chamber has taken notice of what Mr. Lukic said, that if there's any discrepancy between the time estimates in either 92 ter motions or the witness list, that we can rely on always the shorter time; but, Mr. Lukic, in your new witness list, that should become clear already anyhow. I now move to the exhibit list. Filing an exhibit list does not necessarily require all the documents to be uploaded in e-court. These are two separate things. The one is a technical way of dealing with documents in the e-court system; but the primary purpose of filing an exhibit list is to inform the other party about the exhibits the Defence intends to use. Now, if there's no consolidated list yet, and if there is no consolidated list by this Friday, then the Defence should take care that there is a list with duplicates, or not, but the list should be there and should be filed. And if it's, at this moment, still spread over several list, then you put it together with all the risks of duplicates. But the Prosecution is entitled to know what is on that list. That should be filed on the 16th of May. If there are any exhibits later to be used not appearing on that list, the usual procedure applies that the Defence would have to ask for aiding any documents to its exhibit lists and to give the reasons for the late addition to that list. The Chamber understands that filed in this way, that, in the future, some exhibits may be removed because they're duplicates; that is -- the Chamber is aware of that. But we'll not refrain from, at this moment, requiring the Defence from filing an exhibit list. 16th of May, close of business. As far as the weekly reporting is concerned, the Chamber has serious concerns about what it heard this morning, and it will closely monitor in court the progress on the issues discussed this morning but will not do that by requiring a written report every week, but whenever there is an issue, we'll actively inquire with the parties where we stand, what has to be done, et cetera. Finally, as far as the -- One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if we inquire into these matters, of course it should be clear that the Defence should be prepared to give the information. Not to say, I don't know, or someone else deals with it. The Defence should be on top of what happens or what happened when the Chamber asks for information. Finally, I earlier emphasised that uploading into e-court is a very practical thing and important to be done but would not -- if it's not complete yet would not obstruct in filing an exhibit list, but the Chamber was informed that from the logs kept by ITSS that it only happened once that a batch could not be uploaded in e-court and that there was a problem there; whereas, all the other attempts apparently did not create similar problems. I'm stating this clearly because we should distinguish between technical problems and, as I said, organisational problems the Defence may face. These were the matters I would like to -- that go back to what we discussed before the break. If there's any update by the parties on any matter before the break, the Chamber would hear them now and otherwise we'll proceed with the agenda. Then we'll proceed with the agenda. Yes, the Chamber will have to decide on matters under Rule 73 ter. The Defence has been requested to call 336 witnesses, apart from a few to be stricken anyhow, but the Defence did not, in accordance with Rule 65 ter (G), specify the total number of hours it is requesting. The Chamber has calculated, not yet considering the witnesses who have to be stricken from the list, but based on that Rule 65 ter witness list as it was filed until now, that the Defence requests over 300 hours to examine its witnesses. Now, the Defence certainly will be aware that in cases involving a single accused the Defence often is granted even less time than the Prosecution. In this case the Prosecution used 207.5 hours, and the Defence should expect certainly not more - rather, less - time than those 207.5 hours on the basis that the burden is on the Prosecution to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt. And the Chamber invites the Defence to express itself on the 300 hours against the 207.5 hours and what it intends to do about it, because, as I said, it would be fair to expect certainly not more than the number of hours granted to the Prosecution. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have prepared something in B/C/S. With regard to the number of hours that the Defence requested, we have to say that, pursuant to Rule 98 bis, we wanted to exclude some of the incidents from the indictment. However, we know that everything that the accused has been charged with remains. One of the reasons why we need so many hours is that we have to call all the witnesses for all the counts in the indictment. The OTP had over 200 hours viva voce. They had over 200 witnesses pursuant to Rule 98 bis. We have to respond to the statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis, because we have not been allowed to cross-examine those witnesses that have been proposed and accepted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. Obviously we're not sure that we will bring all the witnesses that we have proposed. However, we have to reserve both the time and a place for all of them. For example, in the Karadzic case, the defence spent over 350 hours all together. Some of the witnesses testified in the Karadzic case and in our case they are 92 bis witnesses and we have to respond to their statements. To be honest at this moment we don't know and we do not have a conclusive list of all the witnesses who have been accepted pursuant to Rule 92 bis that the Prosecutor proposed. The Prosecutor has filed a lot of submissions, and, at this moment, we don't know the exact number of the witnesses. I'm sure that there will be changes and amendments to that list and to the number of hours. I can say that, in the meantime, one of the witnesses has died and his statement will be included pursuant to Rule 92 quater. We hope that during our case we will also be able to have some of the witnesses accepted pursuant to Rule 92 bis. However, at this moment, we don't have all of their statements and we cannot make a decision on that issue. Today we have dealt with the issue of 92 ter witnesses and their testimonies. We will make adjustments in that sense and this will also drastically reduce the time. So if we have the right to examine the witness, although he is not a 92 ter and viva voce witness, I believe that most of such witnesses denoted as "mixed" will become witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 ter, and they -- the time for their testimony will be 30 minutes, as has been ordered today by the Trial Chamber. And this would be more or less all that we can say on this issue. This is our explanation for the number of hours that have been requested. So even if the number of hours is restricted, with all due respect, we would kindly ask that our -- the number of our witnesses is not restricted. We will condense the time, but we will still want to be able to make decisions as to what witnesses to bring. And, as I've already told you, at this moment, we do not really know whether we will, indeed, need to bring all of the witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. First of all, even if you have not take a statement yet, of course, it's finally for the Defence to head either for 92 bis or 92 ter. I mean, it's not -- you don't have to wait until everything is completed. And then it's your own approach which allows you to say -- and if one out of 20 or 30 witnesses would move from 92 ter to 92 bis, that's, of course, what happens now and then about. But the overall approach shows at this moment that you have hardly any 92 bis witnesses and almost all of them 92 ter or viva voce. That is different from what the Prosecution did. Now, it's up to the Defence to use the time as they wish, but I understand your submission. If you reduce the time, that is acceptable, but please do not reduce the number of witnesses so that you have still some flexibility in, for example, moving quite a number of witnesses to 92 bis or reducing their time as viva voce witnesses. That is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say, We have to respond, we would have expected that after the Rule 98 bis decision, we would have to deal with less of the charges, of course, this more or less ignores that the Prosecution was in a similar position and had to prove or at least present evidence on all the charges, and if you would say after the 98 bis decision there would be far less remaining, that would then justify a considerable reduction of the time the Defence would need, compared to the time the Prosecution used. But let's stay out of that. The Chamber will consider whether there's -- what time would be granted, whether it would be the same as the Prosecution. The Chamber also expects a witness list to be filed -- a new witness list to be filed this Friday, and we'll let you know in advance, most likely later today, what will be the number of hours, and if we would also limit the number of witnesses, what that number would be. The Chamber -- the Defence will be informed about it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll, without undue delay, inform the Defence on our decisions in this matter. Mr. Groome, was there anything you'd like to add there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with respect to the number of witnesses, there are two categories of witnesses that the Prosecution has some concern that they're on the list; so, for example, there are some witnesses that seem to relate to facts that have already been agreed. So, for example, in the 4th of June, 2013, there is a filing in which the Prosecution entered into agreement with the Mladic Defence that on 16th July, 1995, Mr. Mladic attend add wedding. When we review the list, we see that both the bride and the groom as well as the videographer from that wedding are intended to be called. We don't understand what the relevance is given that we've agreed to that fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was one of the points the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would have raised again, but -- about those same days, but we saw that, I think the -- there was someone on the list who could testify about where Mr. Mladic stayed overnight when he was in Belgrade. That is a fact which is agreed between Prosecution and Defence, so the Chamber also wondered -- and that's apart from the wedding, is a similar detail which we noticed. But before I give you an opportunity, Mr. Lukic, I would first like to allow Mr. Groome to finish what he started to bring to our attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the second category of witnesses that causes us some concern, and there seems to be quite a few of them, are witnesses that provide what is -- is commonly known as tu quoque evidence. For example, RM180 appears to be a victim of a rape that occurred in a prison in Sarajevo. We have trouble struggling to understand how it would be relevant to any of the Chamber's task in adjudicating this indictment or any of the charges in the indictment. Our concern of the anguish it might causes the witness and, of course, with so many witnesses addressing tu quoque evidence, it could be of considerable use of court time which ultimately will prove to be unnecessary in the Chamber's deliberations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, therefore, two issues. The one is what has been agreed upon already by the parties and that at least for the time in Belgrade I would agree that it would cover, well, at least, a number of witnesses who are announced to testify about what happened in those days in Belgrade, whereas from the agreed facts there was one issue remaining that was at what time Mr. Mladic on 17th of July would have left Belgrade and be back in Crna Rijeka. But much of it is already in the agreed facts. And the second issue raised by Mr. Groome is a general issue. That is the relevant of tu quoque evidence, especially to call witnesses to appear before this Court to testify about what Mr. Groome considers to be tu quoque evidence. Could you briefly respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 16th of July, I think that there are some issues about the time when Mr. Mladic left Belgrade. I think that the Prosecution is still claiming that he left Belgrade on the 16th and the Defence is claiming that he left Belgrade on the 17th in the morning. And I see Mr. McCloskey nodding, agreeing, seeing he is the best knowledgeable about the issue. And regarding tu quoque issue, I can tell you what was the overall situation in which crimes occurred, it's not the same if the crime it was organised, ordered, or if it's a consequence of revenge as we pointed out from the beginning of our case. That the revenge and over circumstances might influence the commission of the crime. Not only whether somebody is a member of police or military or paramilitary but also there are certainly acts of revenge during the war. And if you want to connect those acts of revenge, we have to know the whole situation at that time in that area. So we do not consider it that it's tu quoque Defence. It's not. But we want to show you the whole picture. That's the only intention we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it's still not easy to understand. Mr. Groome gave one example, that if a witness appears to have been a victim of a rape that occurred in a prison, how that links directly to what seems to be the core of the Sarajevo case, that is, indiscriminate shelling, et cetera, unless you establish clearly that -- or sniping, that the one has caused the other which is not immediately understandable without further explanation. And apart from that, Mr. Lukic, isn't it true that, especially background information, what may have caused another thing, what may have been in the background, that that is specifically mentioned as the type of evidence which can be presented through 92 bis. And I do not know to what extent there is a challenge to that evidence. It's the relevance which is primarily raised by Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to go back to this witness temporarily marked as GRM180. That's not the only issue she would be testifying. She would testify about the overall situation in Sarajevo city during conflict. Condition -- condition regarding paramilitary units, lack of food, water, and electricity on obviously all sides. So it's only the last issue she would testify on is about her rape. And that probably would be placed together with everything else to have the whole picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've heard your explanation. Mr. Groome, anything to add to that? I understood it not that it would be an incident or one thing where you need a bit of more background evidence to be presented but an overall impression that there was lot of what you consider to be tu quoque.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and just looking at the summaries, and we're somewhat hindered by not having the statements, which hopefully we'll deal with later this morning, but I certainly perhaps -- well, I know that the Prosecution will most definitely in response to specific 92 ter applications will be raising this issues with respect to individual witnesses after we've seen the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I would like to move on. Mr. Lukic, perhaps you could consider through the use of 92 bis to be a bit more to expound on that. The Chamber also noticed that there seems to be some repetition in the proposed evidence sometimes in, for example, a number of expert witnesses on a history of a region, and I'm specifically referring to three -- entries 331, 332, and 336. We dealt already with the agreed facts. The way in which you have presented some of the evidence of those witnesses who can tell us about Belgrade certainly overlaps considerably with what was already agreed. And sometimes extensive time as seems to have been reserved, for example, ballistic reports, many, many hours, ten hours, for example, where you would except to read the most relevant information in their report, rather than in -- to hear it in the examination-in-chief of those witnesses. These are just a few suggestions that might assist you in reconsidering the time you are claiming for Defence witnesses. As I said before, we need a consolidated witness list by the 16th of May, and you should consider that all the guidance the Chamber gave should be clear -- that you took that seriously, should be clear from that new witness list; that is, no anonymous witness, et cetera. Anything else on witness lists? If not, I'll move on. The next item is whether there will be a Defence opening statement. Mr. Lukic, is it the intention of the Defence to make an opening statement; and, if so, how much time you would need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll start saving Court's time from there. We are not going to have our opening statement. We'll proceed with the witnesses immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As of next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's Monday, the 19th of May. I also understand this as no application for Mr. Mladic to make an unsworn statement, which, by the way, is not in the Rules anyhow, but the Chamber is aware that sometimes some chambers considered that beyond what is the Rules that it would be allowed anyhow. But there is no application for that either. That is clear. As I said before, the exhibit list should be filed 16th of May. I move to the next item: Expert reports. Mr. Lukic, could you give us any indication as when you intend to file your first expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that the ballistic expertise is pretty much done, just adjusted to our exhibit numbers, I think. That's what had to be done, and some new documents that occurred during our trial were incorporated. So we are the closest to submit those expert reports, and they are probably the most detailed, but the Prosecution had the -- a chance to see similar from the same people, and presented in Karadzic case. So there wouldn't be big differences in between those two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is clear. Now we do not only have ballistic experts. Could you give an estimate on, for example, ballistic experts within the next four weeks or next six weeks --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Four weeks definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But for the other witnesses, could you also perhaps include in your filing to say we expect expert witness on background -- regional background, for example, by early September or -- so that we have an overview of what reasonably could be expected in terms of expert reports well in advance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I really have no idea and now I have to call the experts back to inquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's -- of course, I wouldn't expect you to do that. If -- by, for example, if you could include that in a filing by this Friday or if it would be the second half the next week, it would not be a major problem for the Chamber. But at least that we have a bit of an idea on what to expect when.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then I set a deadline until Friday, the 26th -- no, the 23rd of May. That is, the end of the week where we start hearing the evidence. Then Rule 67 disclosure. It has already been referred to earlier. The Chamber, in our order of the 26th of February, we have ordered that the Defence shall perform its disclosure obligations pursuant to Rule 67(A) of the Rules no later than the 5th of May, 2014. And there were informal communications from the Prosecution to the Defence earlier this month, pursuant to which the Prosecution asserted that the Defence had not performed its disclosure obligations. Of course, we touched upon it already although in a bit marginal way earlier, but I would first like to invite the Prosecution to make further submissions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply to say that I agree with what -- the Chamber's recounting of the procedural history of this particular matter. As of last Monday we did not receive the -- the disclosure that we were entitled to receive, made several attempts over the course of the week to try to reach Mr. Lukic unsuccessfully to try to identify what the problem was and to find out when we would receive it. As I'm standing here, we still have not received that disclosure nor have we had an explanations or any type of plan proposed as to when we would receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A bit confusion my side. [Interpretation] I will speak in B/C/S again. First of all, we have been following the practice that was adopted by a different Chamber in the Karadzic because the cases are similar, the indictments are approximately the same, and the scope of the Defence is the same. We were following the practice of having the statements signed 48 hours before the testimony. Today we are able to say that over the past few day we have managed to collect signatures for the statements that have already been submitted for translation for the first few witnesses; I believe for two weeks' worth of witnesses, approximately. You will see that are no changes in the statements. They are the same statements. We have sent them for translation, and we thought that by sending them for translation, we have, in fact, disclosed the statements we are going to use. It's just that with this number of people and the position of the team that is in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Perhaps I didn't understand you well. You said by sending the statements for translation, you, in fact, disclosed the statements which you are going to use. Well, CLSS may then be aware of the statement, but disclosure is about the other party in the proceedings who is not aware at all and will not be informed about what you sent for translation. Apart from that, they're entitled to receive that in one of the official languages of the Tribunal - that is, English or French - because otherwise they can't work with it. Disclosure is a vehicle which allows the other party to proceed in preparing for their position at this stage of the proceedings. So, therefore, I'm a bit surprised that you consider sending a document for translation as disclosure to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not clear enough; I apologise. All those statements were disclosed to the Prosecutor in time through a 92 ter submission. They have been translated within the time stipulated by the Rules. So they did receive the statement on time, the statements, in fact, except that they were not signed, so we were not late with disclosing the statements we are going to use. The statements were provided in both languages within the 92 ter submission, and they were all filed within due time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this leads me to two short observations. First of all, although you have to file a statement with a 92 ter motion, you're supposed to disclose the statement of any witnesses if you want to use that statement earlier; that is, the Rule 67(A) disclosure. So to say it's in time, well, that's at least arguable whether it is or is not. That's one. The second issue is, and that seems to be one of the issues that is of some concern to the Prosecution, that the Prosecution fears that if they receive an unsigned statement that they will face at a later stage a statement which is considerably different from what was initially presented. I do understand that as far as the second issue is concerned that you say, Well, the late signature is mainly for practical reasons, and, until now, has not led us to believe that there will be significant changes. Now, if that would be the case, Mr. Groome might have less concerns if this would be practice for the year to come. Mr. Groome might have less concerns but he is not convinced yet that he has a proper -- that he can expect that to happen. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are really two issues that we're talking about here. One is the compliance with Rule 67, and then whether that -- with the 92 ter applications and whether disclosure obligations of the Defence have been met with unsigned draft statements. I'm going to ask Ms. Bibles to deal with that particular issue after I address the Chamber on the question of disclosure. It seems -- I'm not sure that Mr. Lukic appreciates the full boundaries of his obligation. Under Rule 67(A)(ii), they're obliged to provide the Prosecutor copies of statements, if any, of all witnesses whom the Defence intends to call to testify at trial and copies of all written statements taken in accordance with 92 bis and Rule 92 ter. Yes, Mr. Lukic, the Defence have provided approximately 16 or 18 draft statements mostly, I think we have one signed statement, for the first set of witnesses, but for the remainder of the 336 witnesses we have not received anything. And we're entitled to have that so we can see what the Defence case is with respect to people from the Ilidza Brigade or a particular crime. We're entitled to have that so we can formulate our response to the Defence and that's the -- the -- it's those other missing statements that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I made that distinction in the beginning. Mr. Lukic, could you inform us on how many witness statements do you have at all? I mean, you are asking for 336 witnesses, how many witness statements do you have or how many transcript excerpts if want to lead the witness through a 92 ter -- from how many witnesses do you have them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Immediately when we have the statement, we send it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to my question. My question was -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... all we have, we sent already to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're telling us that you have less than 20 statements of the 336 witnesses you intend to call? And you still are saying, are seriously telling us that you are fulfilling your obligations in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The way I read the Rule is that we have to give that to the Prosecution all we have. That's all we have at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If a statement is not there, of course, that creates and we have case law on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there is, of course, a situation where sometimes, perhaps, a statement has not been taken yet; but, under the Rule, at the very beginning: "Copies of statements..." - if any, it really says, I agree with that - "...of all witnesses whom the Defence intends to call to testify at trial and copies of all written statements taken in accordance with Rule 92 bis, 92 ter." Of course, if you call a viva voce witness, there may not be a statement, but the starting point is that you provide the Prosecution with statements, whenever taken, of witnesses you intend to call. Therefore, I do not know exactly what your understanding of the Rule is based upon but that's what the Rule tells us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My understanding that we have to disclose whatever we have and still because of -- we were not able to talk with so many witnesses and to finalise their statements. We have statements taken from them but they are not finalised. There are more. Of course, they have all the statements from Karadzic case. They would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you disclosed them to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We got it from them. We didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are in this proceedings, if you got anything, you have to select -- you have to say we want to call witness

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Witness A has given a statement in Karadzic, in wherever, earlier to whatever authority. These are the statements. They are hereby disclosed to you as relevant material in this ways. That's what the Rule -- Rule tells you to do. Not to say, Well, you know already from another case what statements were ever taken and -- that's not what the Rule is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we'll disclose the statements from Karadzic case they already have. And it's pretty large number of witnesses that would go by those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: By our count there are 122 witnesses from the Karadzic case. Do I understand from Mr. Lukic's statement then, just now, that for Karadzic witnesses the same statement that was proffered in the Karadzic case will be proffered before this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our intention was, of course, to adjust the statements. Some issues are not actually interesting for us. For example, some SDS meetings or Crisis Staff meetings. We wanted to adjust them to our military case, mostly. But if it's the ruling by the Chamber that we disclose those statements, we can disclose the statements as they are and then make the additions to those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'd like to you do is to sit together with Mr. Groome to say: This is what we intend to do. We have statements from Karadzic but we'll date by a red line or whatever that we most likely will skip this and this and this from those statements because they are irrelevant for us, but apart from that that is what remains is then the statement on which we wish to rely. First of all, I want you to abide by the Rules, but second, I want and the Chamber wants you to find practical solutions which enable both parties to prepare for the Defence case and to say, Well, you know it already, how could Mr. Groome guess on what you consider relevant or less relevant in the Karadzic statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He cannot, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. And if you already 120 statements, why not one of the -- you as lead counsel ask for advice from your team members and say, Okay, Karadzic case, this is relevant, that's not relevant, this is not relevant, so just to give Mr. Groome an impression on what he has to prepare for and then he has instead of less than 20 he already has 120 statements which allows him to at least further prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I assist the court reporter. At the moment three microphones were switched on and the court reporter, as you can see from the transcript, asked twice to switch off if they are not used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll switch on my microphone. Mr. Lukic, Mr. Groome also complained -- well, by "complained" he mentioned that he tried to reach you but couldn't reach you in order to further discuss these matters. Mr. Groome, would be it a good idea to see how far you could come if you would meet and try to find practical solutions to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are always willing to meet. I guess I'm concerned that my willingness to meet shouldn't be confused with my still -- my insistence that the Prosecution has certain procedural rights need to be observed. So in this particular case, now we've talked about 122 witnesses and we'll have a discussion about those Karadzic witnesses, but that still leaves 200 statements -- 92 ter statements that I think the Chamber should set a deadline. I mean, we're heard Mr. Lukic say that one of the witnesses has died and the statement will be offered 92 quater, so we know that statement exists. Well, we should have had that last Monday. So any statements that are currently in existence that the Defence intends to tender through 92 bis, ter, or quater were passed due, and I would ask that immediate steps be taken to get us that information, those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is my suggestion to meet. At the basis of that suggestion was that if you received those statements that at the same time you would receive information about what the Defence would most likely not use from those statements so that you were -- be better able to focus on what the Defence intends to focus on later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Certainly that aspect of it is appreciated and we're happy to meet Mr. Lukic, but I'd ask him to address the rest of it, the remaining stuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only to address this issue of this gentleman who died. He testified in Karadzic case also. So it's just transferring his Karadzic statement into 92 quater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I think Mr. Groome hears at this hearing that the witness died instead of having been informed about it before, by name, and so to know that this would be a 92 quater witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I learned this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You learned this morning, then I can't have any criticism on that and I will not. Nevertheless, Mr. Lukic, the Chamber is invited to send a dead-line for the Rule 67(A) disclosure. Do you have any further observations to be made as far as time timing is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to tell that you we really need more time to compose all the statements. If that's the rule that we have to disclose it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the Rules says that any -- any statement given by that witness, even if you want to take out smaller portions later, whatever, but you should disclose statements taken by that witness even if it's not you yourself who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But right now we have it in, like, rough version. It's not sentences. It's just facts put. Now we have to make proper sentences because we -- I speak with the witness and I type. That's how our team-works. We don't have manpower. I don't have a typist or somebody else. I have to type what I speak with that witness, so of course I catch only the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at least for those 120 witnesses statements do exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you tell me that for all the other witnesses no statement of whatever kind exists, I'd be surprised, but it's still possible. But you should try to find whatever statements there are there and to provide them as -- to disclose them as soon as possible to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would be the happiest lawyer in the world if I have all those statements given to the Prosecutor already, trust me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We may set a deadline that you will have to disclose to the Prosecution any existing statement of the witness by a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or maybe it's better if I sit with Mr. Groome first and then inform you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- I think Mr. Groome said sitting together would not resolve this problem, but if you think and if Mr. Groome thinks that waiting for one or two more days to set such a deadline, that we could be assisted by the parties and not making it worse as it is already, then we'll consider that. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour could I just that -- it seems that the Defence has -- there's been some confusion about the extent of their obligation. I would ask the Chamber to instruct them by this Friday to give some consideration to this discussion today and to propose a plan as to when they will be able to meet their Rule 67 obligations. I'm happy to meet with Mr. Lukic at any time and to discuss any issues - and there are many issues - but I will never agree that -- that the requirements of Rule 67 be vitiated. I must insist on that. And I believe it's for Mr. Lukic at this stage now, bearing in mind this discussion, to propose a plan forward to when he will be able to meet his obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber follows this suggestion. That is, the parties are encouraged to meet and that Mr. Lukic presents a plan for Rule 67(A) disclosure with the benefit of having spoken to Mr. Groome on the matter, knowing exactly what his obligations are, and to come up with a plan to be filed this Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Finally, Your Honour, with respect to the witnesses that already testified in Karadzic, I'm happy to talk about them and, of course, we do have access to that evidence. May I ask the Chamber to instruct the Defence that that -- those should be the witnesses that are called until this problem is solved because at least in that case we do have access to the witnesses' evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you willing to give priority to calling those witnesses who have testified already in Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to since we do not have statements for any other witnesses anyways. Only -- only [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I consider this an agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have -- we have three witnesses, sorry for interrupting you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have three witnesses coming soon but their statements were disclosed in a timely manner, so I think it's not in this category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the exception of three witnesses, would that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the 17th of April the Defence notified the Chamber and the Prosecution about a witness order. All of those witnesses we agree we make no objection to them being called, and I believe that Mr. Lukic will confirm that that scheduling of witnesses is still the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Same. We confirmed it this morning [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So prioritising Karadzic witnesses will start after the testimony of those witnesses who have already been scheduled. And, Mr. Lukic, you have agreed to not calling other witnesses but, first, to focus on those witnesses until the 67(A) disclosure issue has been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby on the record. Then I have a few practical matters. First, Rule 92 ter motions. I'd like to take the opportunity for the Chamber to recall its guidance set out at the beginning of the Prosecution case with respect to Rule 92 ter motions and decisions to be taken thereon. But rather than continuing with that, I think we should first take a break. We -- at least the Chamber doesn't need much time after the break. I would consider some 20 minutes or anything between 20 and 30 minutes. I suggest we take a break and that we will resume at 25 minutes to 1.00 and then finish somewhere around 1.00. Unless the parties would have considerable matters to be raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have about ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see nothing right now on our side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll finish in the next session and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
