utterances.text: I think before the break I started saying that the Chamber takes this opportunity to recall its guidance set out at the beginning of the Prosecution case with respect to 92 ter motions and decisions to be taken thereon. The Chamber informs the parties that it shall apply the guidance it set out at transcript pages 2408 to 2410 to the extent that it will only decide on the admission of proffered Rule 92 ter material when the witness appears in court, save for instances where a specific issue raised by the opposing party - and that would be the Prosecution in this case - warrants issuing a decision prior to the witness's appearance. The Chamber hereby puts on the record that on the 7th of May, 2014, it granted the Defence's request for leave to reply to the Prosecution's provisional response to the Defence Rule 92 ter motions and informed the parties accordingly through an informal communication. In the Prosecution's responses to the Defence Rule 92 ter motions for Dragomir Andan and two other witnesses, the Prosecution has claimed that the Defence has failed to provide signed statements for those witnesses. In the Prosecution's view, the statements, when signed, may include substantial amendments and therefore the Prosecution has requested that these witnesses are called viva voce. If the Prosecution wishes to address this matter further, it has an opportunity to do so, and the same would be true for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to restate everything that we put in that response, but essentially our position is if the Defence is unable to meet its obligations under Rule 92 ter and Rule 67, and that is to provide a signed statement, that it seems that procedural fairness requires that the witness simply be called viva voce. This is somewhat unusual set of circumstances where a signed statement is not attached to the 92 ter application or has not been provided and it seems that, again, that viva voce would be the best way to proceed particularly when, and this is also motivated by our analysis of this unsigned document and our analysis in one particular case the witness has said in the past, that there seems to be such a contradiction that it seems that hard to imagine that all that can be resolved, and if it's only resolved the night before the person appears in court here, it seems to inject a certain amount of procedural unfairness to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As I said before, we have signed statements of most of the witnesses that should appear at the beginning of our case. And I hope that we will be able to provide those signatures with no changes in the statements to the Prosecution hopefully today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. The Chamber, at this point in time, will not grant the request by the Prosecution that we should order the Defence to examine the witnesses viva voce. We -- at this stage, we deny that objection, but, of course, we are not knowing exactly what will happen and the Chamber, of course, is also unaware of any previous statements taken from any witnesses which might cause a the-night-before-the-next-day change to that statement. But we will consider that if it comes to it. But the mere fact that they're not signed in itself is no reason for the Chamber to instruct the Defence to examine its witnesses viva voce. At the same time, Mr. Lukic, you will understand that if drastic changes will appear, or if anything happens, the Chamber still has an opportunity to instruct you to examine the witness viva voce if circumstances, indeed, would require us to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then in its provisional response to the Defence Rule 92 ter motions dated 28th April of this year and its provisional response to the Defence's Rule 92 ter motion for Svetozar Guzina, dated the 2nd of May, 2014, the Prosecution stated that it would like, first, to address the Chamber about the practice of tendering written material pursuant to Rule 92 ter; and two, on some clear guide-lines from the Chamber on the procedure to be used when contacting Defence witnesses. Mr. Groome, to the extent the first item needs further explanation, you may give it, and the second issue approaching Defence witnesses has not yet been addressed today, so you have an opportunity to do that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I suggest that perhaps if Mr. Lukic and myself are going to meet, that we discuss this and maybe take a few minutes next week just to raise the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see everybody is nodding, both my colleagues and Mr. Lukic, so we'll further hear from you on these matters after you've met with Mr. Lukic. And I then take it that matters such as tendering portions of statements or testimony which would give an unbalanced view on the matter would be one of the issues you would discuss and also associated exhibits, not flooding the Chamber with associated exhibits. These are all within the subject matter you would like to discuss with the Defence, Mr. Groome. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is true, Your Honour, but there is one matter that you've just touched upon that I would encourage the Chamber to begin considering. And when we look at some of these witness, particularly witnesses who testified in the Karadzic case, that during the cross-examination of those witnesses, in some cases, the witness -- the Prosecution showed the witness maps and had the witness mark the maps, showed some photographs, and the witness marked the photographs, and we -- the Prosecution's position is that that clarified some of the issues in the statement. If we're going to see those statements again, it's likely that we would do the same thing, show the same map, show the same photographs, and just thinking in the long-term of ways to make this process more efficient, the Prosecution considers if, procedurally, we were able to put that line of questioning before the Chamber, there would be no need for us to take Court time in doing that. I think we put it in -- we'd first raise it with the Guzina response. I expect that we'll be doing it in the future. Perhaps at this stage if I could simply ask the Chamber to consider that or to consider alternative ways to perhaps gain some efficiency by where we intend to ask the same questions to simply introduce that. We're still trying to think about it conceptually. Obviously, under 92 ter the witness would be required to listen to their Karadzic testimony and we'd have to lay a foundation. Under 92 bis the witness doesn't have to listen to their prior testimony. It's taken that given sworn testimony can be just tendered under 92 bis. So we're still trying to sort out exactly our thinking on it, but perhaps if the Chamber could also consider -- begin to consider this issue, and we'll raise it in the context of specific filings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we certainly will. And if I understand you well, you're mainly focussing on visualising exercises in support of the testimony or the statement given.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's what we've identified so far. It's possible that we might be suggesting in the future that if it's our intention to do the exact same cross-examination, that those hours could be saved simply by introducing that cross-examination in written form. Of course, if it's the -- the Karadzic statement that's now going to be tendered, it's likely that a large percentage of our questions will be identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll certainly start considering these modalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll -- have started considering it already, and we'll continue to do so. Then, I'd like to move into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If the Defence notifies the Prosecution and the Chamber of existing protective measures for any of its witnesses, it should clearly indicate which protective measures were granted, by which -- which Chamber, and refer, make a reference, to that specific decision of that Chamber. I move on. The Chamber hereby informs the parties that the Chamber will not be able to sit on the 30th of June and the 1st of July of this year. That's a Monday and a Tuesday. I move to my next agenda item. The Chamber noted that the B/C/S version of Witness RM311's witness statement - and that is Exhibit P3520 - includes photographs which do not appear to have been tendered or admitted. Considering, however, that the English version of the statement makes reference to these photographs, the Chamber is satisfied that the photographs should also form part of the exhibit. And the Chamber therefore considers the entirety of P3520 to be in evidence. I move to some translation matters, and I will first deal with P3653, P3654, and P3655. On the 13th of March of this year, the Chamber informally requested the Prosecution to upload into e-court the English translations of Exhibits P3653, P3654, and P3655 admitted into evidence through Witness Milenko Tomic. On the 7th of April, the Prosecution informed the Chamber about the uploading of these translations into e-court under doc IDs 0614-7784-ET, 0307-5580-1, and 0307-5581 respectively. The Chamber hereby instructs the Court Officer to attach the newly uploaded translation of Exhibits P3653, P3654, and P3655 to the respective B/C/S originals. I'll now deal with Exhibit P1756. The Prosecution has uploaded a revised B/C/S translation of P1756 into e-court under doc ID R068-5514-1 B/C/S. The Chamber hereby instructs the Court Officer to replace the existing B/C/S translation of Exhibit P1756 with the revised one. I've exhausted my agenda and give an opportunity to the parties to raise whatever matter they feel they should raise. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. According to the Chamber's guidance and the practice during the Prosecution case, we gave the Defence notice of the documents or exhibits that be used with the witness a week in advance. The Defence have provided us some associated exhibits for the witnesses next week, so my query is whether is that the totality of the exhibits that will be used with the witness's next week; if it's not, can we be given notice of what other exhibits will be used with those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's totality of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a short and clear answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The second matter is, Your Honour, relates to translations. I don't believe we've heard from Defence today whether they are in possession of the necessary translations. When we look in e-court, it appears that there are some missing, so perhaps it would be useful to hear from the Defence: Are they experiencing problems with translations or do they anticipate being able to -- to provide those when needed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give us one second. I'm just consulting with my colleague, Ivetic. We are not aware of any translations missing for the witnesses coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's about others from the 1900 exhibits uploaded into e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I know that for some associated exhibits we could not find a corresponding translation, and Ms. Stewart just informs me that there seems to be maybe some disconnect between the document itself that's intended to be tendered as well as the translation. If I could ask maybe at this stage for Defence to investigate the matter and hopefully by next Monday it will be sorted so we will be able to find documents. It has implications for our preparation because we obviously need to read the translation to prepare for the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome, if you would be able to already point at the most urgent ones you would need so the Defence could start exploring those specific documents and then later come back to you, and it's appreciated that the parties will try to resolve the problem among ourselves. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, this relates to the minimum quantum of information that we need with respect to witnesses to conduct investigations in preparation for our examination. For example, Witnesses GRM198 and GRM202, there's no first name provided. We obviously need the witness's full name. We also need the witness's father name, date of birth, and place of birth to conduct even the most rudimentary investigation. The Prosecution requests that the Chamber order the Defence to provide this information or in the alternative to provide the contact details of the witness that so we can contact them and ask them for it ourselves. I would ask that priority be given to those witnesses who have not testified previously before the Tribunal, those witnesses we are able to find some information and that information has been provided in many cases in the other cases. Obviously, if it is our -- if the first opportunity we have to positively identify the person that comes before the Chamber is when we get to ask our questions on cross-examination, it is likely that we'll be seeking to re-call the witness because it is only then that we can begin our investigations in earnest to verify and then subsequently test the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we could also be provided with the names of the witnesses where this data is missing because I know that I -- when I compose the statement I always put those data.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's the name of the father, the date of birth, and the place of birth as is customarily put in all OTP witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And two specific witnesses were mentioned. Were they mentioned for -- as examples only?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Those were two cases where not even a first name was provided, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And for the others, also father's name, date, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I was informed by Mr. Ivetic that those two are Russian witnesses and we don't have it. They are foreign witnesses. We asked from Russian embassy to be provided with those data, and as soon as we have the data we'll provide the OTP with the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And those reports were actually my -- made by the OTP. It's P9 -- 797. Those are -- authored by those witnesses. And it's on the list. It's in regards to the Markale case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure what we're speaking about at the moment. If that's a reference in a Prosecution document to those two witnesses, thank you, and we will look at that, but as a general rule for the remaining 334 witnesses we would need this additional information to even be able to do any searches in our own systems or make any inquiries about who the person is and what positions they held.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know about the father's name and date of birth should be there. I'm not sure about the place of birth. I don't -- I -- I didn't ask my witnesses. I just asked about their residence now. But we'll talk with Mr. Groome and try to sort this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's sufficient, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's appreciated. Let me just have one look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen that these two are FNU'd on the witness list. If they are authors of any document which is in evidence, then we still might not have their first names because sometimes authors are not mentioning the first name, but it may give a clue, Mr. Groome, and Mr. Lukic certainly will assist you and further find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think there was one other issue about biographical details; that is, the Prosecution has responded to the Defence Rule 92 ter motion for Witness GRM251, and I think the Prosecution has asked for postponement of this witness because the Prosecution wished to receive further biographical information and the correct name of that witness. But I think the Defence has not yet given its position in relation to that request. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And informally we've asked the Defence to do the same thing with respect to two other witnesses that were unknown to us and their names seem -- that we needed to clarify, and so we've asked for three witnesses who have never testified before this Tribunal in any case, that they be postponed to give us some reasonable period of time to investigate who they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they are scheduled for when?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They -- they are in the second set of witnesses that Mr. Lukic tendered, but he hasn't told us when he expects to call them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, postponement, if we do not know exactly when they will be called, do you want the Chamber to already decide on that or rather wait for Mr. Lukic to see whether he could provide you on short notice with the information you are seeking?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's why we dealt with it informally and we only put it in this response. We thought that it merited being included. But they are witnesses GRM251, 020, and 146. Those three witnesses are the witnesses we've asked. Once we get the information we need, we'll take reasonable steps to investigate who they are and we'll report to the Chamber and to the Defence as soon as we've done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you reserve your position as asking for postponement of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- calling those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we could hear from Mr. Lukic when he -- if he has scheduled them. If he has, then that would affect my answer right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those witnesses were scheduled for the second -- one. One is seconded for the second week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you have the information Mr. Groome is seeking available or?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, rather than wasting the Court's time I'll speak with Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is some confusion about the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is any remaining issue, the Chamber would like to be informed as soon as possible, but at this moment we'll refrain from deciding on any request for postponement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that matter is. Mr. Groome, any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any matter to be raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I promised I don't have any, but I think I have to go back to alibi witnesses shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The problem with alibi is not only where General Mladic was at that time but also what he did. The present argument is that he had communications and that probably inferring that he could command, and so we have to explain what he did, where exactly he was, and what kind of communications he was -- had available, if any. So it's not only matter of where was he but also what he did. So that's why if you find those witnesses again on the list, it's not that we are not following your suggestions but because we really need for our case to prove those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it was not very clear from the summary of the witness statement. If it says: The witness will tell us where Mr. Mladic slept that night, and if that's an agreed fact then, of course, there is no need to hear that evidence. But if there is any additional evidence which is relevant and which is not yet covered by the agreed facts, then, of course, it's a different situation, but perhaps the summary may have confused us then a bit. We'll see and hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber still owes you one decision and that is on the number of hours which is granted to the Defence to present its Defence case, and that is exactly the same number of hours as granted to the Prosecution. That is, 207.5 hours. And the number of witnesses is not set further, is not limited by the Chamber. The Defence [sic], I think, all together presented the evidence of some 360 witnesses. The Defence is now asking for 336. And within the time-limits, the Chamber does not further set a limit on the number of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Only one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would just kindly ask, but probably we can sit with Mr. Groome, Mr. McCloskey, the estimate for cross so we can plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can imagine that if they have the statements that it would be far easier to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- [Overlapping speakers] an estimate. But for the first few witnesses it was quite common that the estimates for cross-examination would be given so that the Defence is better able to prepare and organise the appearance of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the best I can say at this stage is the Chamber's guidance with respect to 92 ter witnesses that the cross-examination would be two and a half hours. At this stage I don't think we'll be asking for any more time, but certainly once we have a signed statement we can make a more informed decision about what we need to do on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll send all the signatures we have today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then as soon as possible the Prosecution will provide an estimate of the time needed for cross-examination. This will then conclude the Pre-Defence Conference, but I see that Mr. Mladic would like to consult with counsel. If he would first switch off his microphone, then that would certainly help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any matter to be raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just reminded by a colleague that in our first nine responses we did include an estimate of the time that we would require for cross. So that information has already been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must have overlooked that. Then we will adjourn, and we'll resume, Monday, the 19th of May, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of May, 2014, at 9.30 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
